lines.caption: Avery and Blake both use your expense app. How does Rayfin make sure each of them only sees their own expenses?
One rule on the entity, and the server checks it on every request, row by row.
Hi, I'm Ray! Welcome back to Learn Rayfin with Ray.
Today: who can do what, the policy that keeps each person's rows their own, and why a filter in your app isn't security. Let's dive in!
A permission decorator on an entity says who can use it. Rayfin has two built-in roles: authenticated and anonymous.
The authenticated decorator is for people who are signed in. It takes the actions they get: create, read, update or delete.
A star means all four. The authenticated decorator is shorthand for the role decorator from lessons four and five: same rule, easier to read.
The anonymous decorator is for people who aren't signed in. On Fabric, a tenant admin has to allow anonymous data access first.
But a star alone lets every signed-in person reach every row. Expenses are money people spent: Blake shouldn't see Avery's taxi rides.
So the decorator gets a policy: a function that compares the person asking with each row.

lines.said: claims dot sub is the signed-in person's ID. It has to equal the row's owner underscore I D, or the row is out of reach.
lines.caption: claims.sub is the signed-in person's ID. It has to equal the row's owner_id, or the row is out of reach.
Both sides are typed. Claims has sub, email and role, and item has your entity's fields, so a typo won't compile.

lines.said: The policy checks owner underscore I D, but doesn't fill it in. When your app creates an expense, it sets owner underscore I D from the session.
lines.caption: The policy checks owner_id, but doesn't fill it in. When your app creates an expense, it sets owner_id from the session.
Time for a deep dive! What if an entity has no permission decorator at all?
It isn't locked. Rayfin gives it a default: anyone signed in can create, read, update and delete every row.
Say your app only asks for the signed-in person's expenses. Avery sees just hers. It looks private.
But that filter lives in your app. Blake can ask the same question without it, and get everyone's rows.
He can edit Avery's taxi ride, or delete it, and the server says yes.
Now add the policy. Blake gets only his own rows. Editing or deleting Avery's fails, and so does creating one in her name.
A filter in your app picks which rows to show. A policy on the server decides which rows anyone can reach.
In Fabricator, Blueprint's Data model view gives every entity an access dot: row-scoped, any signed-in, or public.
Here, Report has no permission decorator. Its card says no explicit roles, its dot is any signed-in, and it offers Harden.
Harden asks Copilot to add a row-level policy. After the chat turn, Fabricator redeploys, as always.
Pop quiz! Your app filters out other people's expenses, so nobody sees them. Are they private?
A, yes: the app never shows them. B, yes, as long as everyone has to sign in. Or C, no: only a policy on the server keeps them private.
Pause the video, and guess…
It's C! Anyone signed in can ask without your filter. The policy is what the server checks.
Let's recap. Give every entity a permission decorator: who, and which actions.

lines.said: Keep personal rows private with a policy on claims dot sub. And filter in your app to show rows, never to protect them.
lines.caption: Keep personal rows private with a policy on claims.sub. And filter in your app to show rows, never to protect them.
Your challenge: send this prompt in Fabricator, then find the new entity's access dot in Blueprint's Data model.
Then tell me in the comments: which access does its dot show?
Next time: reading and writing your data, from the query chain to create, update and delete. See you in the water!
Psst… a ray can lie half-buried in the sand and keep breathing, through openings on top of its head. Out of sight, like other people's rows!
